hoverDefinition: Sensitivity changes one assumption, scenarios combine coherent assumptions, and reverse DCF solves what a supplied price would require. These tools expose dependence; they do not assign probabilities or prove a forecast.

covered: One-variable and two-variable comparisons, coherent scenarios, simple reverse-DCF algebra and uncertainty interpretation.
deferred: Probabilistic simulation, full multi-stage reverse DCF, forecast calibration and investment recommendation are deferred.

objectives.statement: Compare valuation assumptions and solve a simple implied cash requirement.
objectives.evidence: Keep other inputs fixed for sensitivity and distinguish a required forecast from an observed fact.

context.timeframe: Independent fictional teaching scenarios. Worked examples and practice start separately; they are not consecutive company-case rounds.
assumptions: Use the simple current-value stable FCFF model V = next-year FCFF/(r−g), with r>g.
Next-year FCFF is supplied after sustainable reinvestment; growth begins after that cash flow.
In one-variable sensitivity, hold the supplied next-year cash and all other inputs fixed. Scenarios explicitly state all changes.
All values/prices are hypothetical; no scenario probability or forecast truth is inferred.

framework.limitations: Conceptual teaching assumptions, with INR lakh as a unit rather than a jurisdiction. No tax rate, financing term, reporting classification, valuation input or management buffer is a current rule or market recommendation. Applicable framework, jurisdiction, reporting period and effective amendments require separate study.

mechanism.title: Ask which assumption changed
paragraphs: A sensitivity changes one driver while holding the others fixed, such as WACC at constant next-year FCFF and growth. A two-way table changes two named drivers in a grid. Recompute every affected formula; do not paste old terminal amounts into a changed-rate model.

For the supplied stable model, a higher r or lower g reduces positive-cash value when other inputs are fixed. Near r=g, small changes create very large swings. The table is a map of assumptions, not evidence that every cell is equally plausible.

mechanism.title: Keep combined assumptions coherent
paragraphs: A scenario changes a set of linked operating and risk assumptions, such as lower cash generation and higher required return. Name the case and its inputs. Do not call unrelated best values a coherent upside or attach probabilities without evidence.

Use the same claims, date, currency and model across cases. Explain the operating reason for changes and identify which assumptions drive the difference rather than treating the range as a statistical confidence interval.

mechanism.title: Solve the supplied value’s implied requirement
paragraphs: A reverse DCF treats a hypothetical operating value as an input and solves for an unknown forecast driver. In this simple model, implied next-year FCFF = operating value×(r−g). More complex models may require solving a multi-period forecast.

The implied cash is what the assumed price/rate/growth combination requires. It is not a forecast guaranteed by the price, proof of overvaluation or a probability. Compare the requirement with operational evidence and feasible reinvestment.

distinctions.name: Sensitivity and scenario
distinctions.explanation: One isolates a driver; the other changes a stated group.

distinctions.name: Range and confidence interval
distinctions.explanation: A set of assumed outputs does not establish outcome probabilities.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Do not give an uncertainty band a statistical claim without evidence.

distinctions.name: Reverse requirement and prediction
distinctions.explanation: Solving an input from a price does not show the input will occur.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Use the result as a question for business evidence.

workedExample.setup: Base model uses next-year FCFF 12, WACC 10%, growth 2% and V = FCFF1/(r−g). A rate-only sensitivity uses WACC 12% with cash/growth unchanged. A downside scenario uses FCFF1 10, WACC 12% and growth 1%. Separately ask what next-year cash a hypothetical operating value 180 requires at base rates.
steps: Rate-only sensitivity = 12/(0.12−0.02) = 120, a decline 30 with other inputs fixed.
This downside changes cash, risk/return and growth; it is not a one-variable result.
For supplied operating value 180 at base rates, implied next-year FCFF = 180×(0.10−0.02) = 14.4.
The required 14.4 exceeds the base assumption 12; that is a modelling requirement to investigate, not proof of a future result.
workedExample.result: Base 150; rate sensitivity 120; downside 90.91; reverse requirement 14.4.
workedExample.interpretation: Each number answers a different question about assumptions and should retain its label.

statementEffects.explanation: Effects under the stated simplified scenario. Forecasts and economic values do not themselves create accounting entries.

misconceptions.claim: Change WACC but keep a model-derived terminal value frozen.
misconceptions.correction: Recompute all formulas depending on the changed assumption.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Which denominator or terminal input depends on this rate?

misconceptions.claim: A chosen scenario range is a statistical confidence interval.
misconceptions.correction: Assumption cases do not establish probabilities.

misconceptions.claim: An implied cash requirement is a forecast fact.
misconceptions.correction: Reverse DCF solves a condition, not its likelihood.
misconceptions.diagnostic: What operational evidence supports meeting it?

practice.setup: Independent stable model: next-year FCFF 8, growth 2%. Compare WACC 10% and 12%, holding the supplied next-year cash and growth fixed; V = FCFF1/(r−g).
practice.question: Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Value stays 100 because the cash forecast is unchanged
options.feedback: The discount-rate spread is part of the model.
Base = 8/(0.10−0.02) = 100; higher-rate value = 8/(0.12−0.02) = 80. This is a controlled sensitivity, not a probability interval.

options.text: 80 to 100 is the model’s confidence interval
options.feedback: No probabilities or statistical coverage have been supplied.

practice.solution: Base = 8/(0.10−0.02) = 100; higher-rate value = 8/(0.12−0.02) = 80. This is a controlled sensitivity, not a probability interval.

hints.text: Change the rate in the denominator and retain the other inputs.
Base = 8/(0.10−0.02) = 100; higher-rate value = 8/(0.12−0.02) = 80. This is a controlled sensitivity, not a probability interval.

practice.setup: Independent reverse-DCF exercise: hypothetical operating value 150, matched WACC 12% and perpetual growth 2%. Use the stable next-year cash model. A separate analyst forecast is next-year FCFF 12.
practice.question: What implied next-year cash and interpretation follow?

options.text: Implied FCFF 15; it is guaranteed to occur because the value is 150
options.feedback: Reverse DCF does not establish a forecast’s truth.

options.text: Implied FCFF 15; the supplied value requires more cash than the separate forecast 12
options.feedback: Implied FCFF = 150×(0.12−0.02) = 15. The separate forecast 12 would support value 120 under those rates. The gap identifies a requirement to investigate, not a guaranteed outcome.

options.text: Implied FCFF 12; preserve the forecast when solving the price requirement
options.feedback: That freezes the unknown rather than solving the model.

practice.solution: Implied FCFF = 150×(0.12−0.02) = 15. The separate forecast 12 would support value 120 under those rates. The gap identifies a requirement to investigate, not a guaranteed outcome.

hints.text: Rearrange value = cash/spread to solve for cash.
Implied FCFF = 150×(0.12−0.02) = 15. The separate forecast 12 would support value 120 under those rates. The gap identifies a requirement to investigate, not a guaranteed outcome.

rubric: Do not turn algebra into a prediction.

sources.title: Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern: Estimating Terminal Value
supports: Background on horizon value, stable-growth versus liquidation assumptions and sustainable terminal inputs. All growth, cash and rate values here are hypothetical, not current economic forecasts.
